title: Student Learns to Walk and Talk Again After Accidental Paracetamol Overdose
excerpt: Riley Lubas, 20, suffered multiple organ failure after unknowingly doubling up on paracetamol. After life support and months of rehab, he is walking and talking again.
body:
• Riley Lubas, 20, a first-year university student in Bath, England, suffered multiple organ failure after unknowingly taking two over-the-counter medicines that both contained paracetamol.
  • He was placed on life support and dialysis at King's College Hospital in London, and topped the UK's liver transplant list — before his liver began recovering on its own.
  • After weeks of intensive care and a tracheostomy, Riley had to relearn to walk and talk. He has since made remarkable progress, though recovery was grueling.
  • The case is a warning for every medicine cabinet: check ingredient labels, because the same active drug is sold under different names in cold and flu products.

A bad cold in his first year at university nearly cost Riley Lubas his life. The 20-year-old student from Newport, studying creative media at the University of Bath, caught a springtime cold in March 2025 and reached for two over-the-counter medicines. He did not realize both contained paracetamol. Within days he was in organ failure, on life support, and at the top of the UK's liver transplant list.

It started, as Riley described it, as something utterly ordinary. "It felt pretty non-eventful. People get freshers' flu or colds all the time in first year, so I got two medicines," he said. "I didn't realise at the time that both had paracetamol in them." When stomach pains set in and he couldn't keep food down, he called the NHS 111 helpline, which directed him to A&E — already sick, he had assumed the stomach pain was a stomach bug and hadn't noticed the pain in his liver specifically.

From the emergency room to life support

Tests at the Royal United Hospital revealed his liver was in trouble. Riley was transferred to King's College Hospital in London, one of Britain's leading liver centers. Within hours of arriving in the ICU he went into multiple organ failure and was placed on life support and dialysis.

Staff at King's began asking his family about his medicine intake. A friend at university found packets of paracetamol and cold-and-flu medication in his room — the missing piece. Doctors suspected an overdose, and Riley was placed at the top of the UK's liver transplant list because, as medics told his parents Chris and Kate, the damage to his liver was "as good as irreversible."

Then came a cruel twist: damage to his heart meant he couldn't safely undergo the transplant for two full days, leaving the family in agonizing limbo. Studies show up to 80 percent of people who suffer multiple organ failure do not survive.

The recovery nobody expected

Against all odds, Riley's liver slowly began to improve on its own. Doctors credited his youth and underlying good health, and after a week he was able to come off dialysis and life support.

"It was mad how quickly it all escalated. I'm just so grateful that I was able to come out the other end alright."

— Riley Lubas, student

But survival was only the start. Riley had undergone a tracheostomy — a surgical procedure to help air reach his lungs — and the toll of organ failure on his body was immense. He had to learn to walk and speak again. "He physically couldn't move once he'd come out of sedation," his father Chris said. "And they had to get him used to being able to breathe without the tracheostomy again. It was like he was suffocating when he was trying to breathe."

After weeks of recovery, Riley was transferred to a hospital back in Newport, where he initially battled severe swelling and muscle loss from being confined to a hospital bed. Month by month, he rebuilt — and today he has learned to walk and talk again.

The warning in every medicine cabinet

The case has become a textbook example of a danger health authorities have long flagged: accidental paracetamol overdose. Cold and flu medicines frequently already contain the painkiller, sold under different brand names, so people can take the same active ingredient twice without knowing it. Taking more than double the recommended adult maximum dose — as Riley had — can cause toxic by-products to build up, damaging the liver and kidneys. In severe cases it causes liver failure, and can be fatal.

The worrying part is that an overdose may not feel like an emergency at first. Symptoms can be limited to sickness, vomiting or stomach pain — or nothing at all in the early stages. That is why Britain's NHS advises anyone who thinks they have taken too much paracetamol to seek medical help immediately, even if they feel completely fine. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has warned that "simple misunderstandings" about medicines can have serious consequences, and has urged everyone to check ingredient lists before combining products.

For families everywhere — including the diaspora households that keep both paracetamol and cold remedies on hand for students living away from home — Riley's story is a one-line lesson worth passing on: read the label, every time. The medicine that feels the safest is often the one people check the least.
image_caption: Riley Lubas with his mother Kate at King’s College Hospital in London. The 20-year-old suffered multiple organ failure after accidentally overdosing on paracetamol and had to relearn to walk and talk.
